moves.speaker: Joshua Rasmussen
moves.proposition: Dependent things collectively require a non-dependent basis; indefinitely many dependent members do not make their total independent.

sourceSpan.excerpt: So this argument has two parts. The first part seeks to explain dependent things. So if you have a dependent sequence of turtles and there's a question about how those turtles exist and why they exist, then the idea is that you're not going to appeal to those very dependent things to explain their existence because that would be circular. So without a foundational reality, there would be no explanation or basis for the existence of dependent things in total. This premise does not depend on the the number of things. No matter how many things there are, whether one or many, the idea is that they would all collectively depend on something prior. It's like if you had a floor with brown tiles, and the floor is, you could say, brown, it doesn't matter how many brown tiles there are. Even if there were infinitely many, the floor in total would still be brown. Same with dominoes that are knocking each other down on a table. If you have infinitely many dominoes, they only knock each other down on that table if there's a table to support them. Now for any dependent things there is a basis for their existence. I'm going to point to three types of reasons for this. I think from reason just reflecting on the nature of dependence. Adding up more dependent things does not yield an independent total. I think this is also supported by experience. Um we've got lots of examples of dependent things. You add them together and they don't form something independent. And then from the expectation of a deeper explanation. I think there's a track record in science to seek a deeper explanation of things. And so we could put this modestly. Uh other things being equal expect a further explanation. And from this it follows that we can expect an explanation of the total of dependent things. And this gives us a reason to think there's a foundational reality.
